claims.text: Mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA powder can be applied to a stainless-steel surface as feedstock for a repair layer.
FSP can consolidate pre-placed HEA particles into a substrate surface.
Approximately 600 rpm and 100 mm/min are suitable FSP parameters for consolidating CoCrFeNiMo0.85 powder on stainless steel.
Real-time temperature and load monitoring can ensure complete and homogeneous powder consolidation.
The proposed FSP operation can be maintained below a peak temperature of 800°C.
Frictional heating and tool-induced deformation plasticize the substrate and mix HEA particles throughout the tool-affected region.
Severe plastic deformation during FSP induces dynamic recrystallization and produces an ultrafine-grained layer.
FSP can consolidate the powder without reaching melting temperatures.
The processed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 layer will be metallurgically bonded to stainless steel and free of cracks.
Avoiding melting eliminates the conditions responsible for hot cracking.
The FSP-produced ultrafine grain structure will increase microhardness relative to untreated stainless steel.
A CoCrFeNiMo0.85 surface layer will improve corrosion resistance in 3.5 wt.% NaCl relative to an untreated stainless-steel surface.
The HEA-containing repair layer will improve wear resistance relative to an untreated substrate.
The proposed FSP repair will have fewer hot cracks and better hardness, corrosion resistance, and wear resistance than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is an applicable corrosion-test environment for CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coatings on stainless steel.
The repaired surface is suitable for service testing in high-temperature oxidative atmospheres.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs of the targeted damaged stainless-steel components are prone to hot cracking.
Tool design, FSP parameters, powder characteristics, and residual stress can materially affect consolidation and final properties.
SEM/EDS, Vickers microhardness, potentiodynamic polarization, and pin-on-disk testing can be used to evaluate the proposed repair against fusion-welded and untreated controls.
The hypothesis is falsified by defective or cracked consolidation, absence of statistically significant property improvements, or failure of process control to mitigate residual stress and cracking.
